newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Experts tip German debt as benchmark.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Experts tip German debt as benchmark.

text.p: Despite French ambitions, German debt is expected to retain its traditional role as European benchmark for bond yield comparisons after European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999, a Reuters survey showed.
Just over half of those who contributed to the monthly survey of EMU expectations, 26 out of 45, agreed that German debt would remain the benchmark.
Only five of those surveyed said they believed a German benchmark was not necessarily a foregone conclusion.

Most respondents to the survey, carried out between February 5 and 6, said Germany would retain its position because of its size, the dominance of its bond market and because it had stronger fundamentals than France.
"Private and public issuers also have higher credit ratings on their debt than their French counterparts," said Gerhardt Grebe, chief economist at Bank Julius Baer.
France has said that as from January 1 1999, when EMU begins, all government debt will be redenominated into euros, the new single currency. Germany has made no similar commitment.
This would give France the lead it needs to establish its debt as the benchmark, say its supporters.

"If France converts its debt into euros from the start of EMU, while German government debt remains in marks, French debt will have to be the benchmark until German debt is converted," said John Arrowsmith, senior research fellow at the British National Intitute of Economic and Social Research.
Some analysts say Germany may find difficulty in converting its debt into euros from 1999, given public resistance to relinquishing a strong and proven currency.

Other aspects of the German bond market tend to bode well for France's benchmark bid. Liquidity at the short end of the yield curve in France is much deeper, making it easier and cheaper to deal than in Germany.

There is also the general perception that the French market is more transparent because it has a primary dealer system which Germany lacks, which underwrites government debt and distributes to private investors.
"This primary dealer system makes it easier to schedule and auction debt," one contributor to the survey said.
Two of the respondents expected a mix of benchmarks from France and Germany. Twelve did not respond to the question.
